en: Homage to the glorious Hevajra!
Having paid homage with devotion to the glorious Hevajra and also to Nairātmyā,
I shall describe the method for his sādhana by the grace of the Vajrācārya.

First of all, the yogin— whose mind is intent upon the welfare of all sentient beings— having properly propitiated the venerable guru and entered the maṇḍala as prescribed in the *Śrī Hevajra*, having been consecrated according to the traditional sequence, and having been duly authorized,

attains the perfectly pure and unerring knowledge of reality and acquires the [auspicious] signs. Then, desiring to accomplish the glorious *Hekāravajra*, he should dwell in a delightful place such as a cremation ground.
Possessing knowledge and observing the commitments (*samaya*) such as the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), having performed the offerings and worship and so forth,
one should visualize a blue-colored syllable *HŪṂ* arising from the letter *Ra* in one's own heart and situated upon a sun disk.

From that *hūṃ* syllable, one should emanate five-colored rays of light into the expanse of space; having drawn [the deities] forth with those rays, one should meditate in the space before oneself upon the Blessed One Vajrajanman—blue in color, with the faces, arms, and weapons to be described, possessing sixteen, six, four, or two arms, embraced by his consort (svavidyā), three-eyed, with tawny hair standing erect, endowed with the six mudrās, surrounded by eight goddesses, and whose form consists of radiating and reabsorbing [light].

In front of him is Gaurī, black in color, with the moon of the bodhicitta in her hand; to the south is Caurī, of madder-red hue, holding in her hand a sun known as the *svayambhū* flower; behind him is Vettālī, red, holding a vessel of vajra-water in her hand; to the north is Ghasmarī, dark green, holding secret medicine; in the northeast is Pukkasī, blue, holding various kinds of meat; in the southeast is Śabarī, white, holding a vessel of elixir in her hand; in the southwest is Caṇḍālī, smoke-colored, playing a *kṛpīṭa* drum; and in the northwest is Ḍombī, of variegated color, embracing her own body.

Having beheld the Blessed One in such a state, his body radiating and withdrawing light, in the sky, one should worship him with the specific outer and secret reality-offerings emerging from the seed-syllable situated upon the sun in one’s own heart; then, in his presence, one should perform the confession of misdeeds and so forth.

Whatever evil karma I have committed in beginningless saṃsāra, produced by unreal conceptualization— that I now confess all before the Blessed One, so that it shall not be done again; and whatever is the merit of all sentient beings—
Having rejoiced in all that, I dedicate it toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Then, having taken refuge in the Buddha, the Blessed One, who is the nature of the entire triple world and consists of the *he*-syllable vajra in the form of great bliss; in the Dharma, which is the essential nature of the mantras, mudrās, maṇḍalas, and so forth taught by him; and in the assembly of deities residing in his wheel—having thus done so, and having correctly resolved the mind upon enlightenment characterized by emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects, which serves as the cause for accomplishing the welfare of all sentient beings, one should cultivate great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) toward all sentient beings, characterized by the love one feels for an only son.

Thereafter, seeing all sentient beings submerged in the ocean of conceptual construction and without refuge, and having brought to manifestation great compassion whose very nature is the desire to deliver them, the mantra-practitioner—having thus attained great joy and disregarding all imagined objects and so forth—should recite the mantra that encapsulates the essential reality of all things: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the knowledge of emptiness. Immediately thereafter, while bringing the meaning of the mantra to manifestation, he should meditate upon himself and the three realms as being without appearance (*nirābhāsa*).

Then, recollecting his vow (*praṇidhi*), he should visualize in the sky a solar disc arising from the syllable *repha*. In its center, he should see a crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*) with five rays, consisting of three prongs, produced from the syllable *hūṃ*. From its rays, he should perceive a blazing vajra-fence, extending as far as he desires, and within that, he should meditate upon a vajra-canopy (*vajrapañjara*).

Having dispelled the obstacles, one should visualize within their midst a white Prajñā in the form of the syllable *E*, pervading space. Above that, one should visualize the earth as a green square born from the syllable *Laṃ*.
Then, a white circular maṇḍala born from the syllable *Vaṃ*.
Then there is the triangular, red fire-maṇḍala born from the syllable *raṃ*;
then the blue air-maṇḍala, shaped like a half-moon, born from the syllable *yaṃ*.
Then, [he] should stabilize that which has the characteristic of emptiness, which is of one taste in the form of great bliss.

Having correctly ascertained the Blessed One, his wheel, and his assembly within awakening characterized by emptiness, one should meditate upon the triple world as being gathered by equanimity and compassion that rescues all those submerged [in saṃsāra]. In the center, one should visualize an extensive lattice-work; in the middle, a square and circular space-form arising from the syllable *laṃ*. Then, having recognized the consciousness situated in the midst of the colors *raṃ*, *yaṃ*, and *vaṃ*, and having transformed all this, one should instantly meditate upon the luminous abode of the maṇḍala circle.
One should clearly visualize [the palace] as square, with four doors, adorned with eight pillars, and decorated with necklaces, half-necklaces, archways, and so forth.

In its center, within the union of the moon and sun, one should see the two seed-syllables *hūṃ* and *aṃ*, from which arise a skull-cup and a flaying knife; above these are the two seed-syllables of the God and Goddess.

One should perceive oneself as the complete transformation of all these, in the form of the glorious *Hevajra*, blue in color, with eight faces, sixteen arms, and four legs, merged in a state of supreme bliss and great pleasure through the union of amorous play with Nairātmyā.
Then: Oṃ! O Lotus, support of bliss, bestower of the bliss of great passion, you who partake in the four joys, O Viśva! Hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ! Accomplish my purpose!
Oṃ! O Vajra, great hatred, bestower of the four joys, whose mouth is the sky and whose single flavor is the Lord; hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ, accomplish my task!
Even in the external ritual of sexual union (suratavidhi), this consecration of the lotus and the vajra must be performed.

Having transformed the [syllable] *āgāram* (the hub of the wheel) into the mandala, which is luminous, clearly manifest with four [petals], and joined in union (*sampuṭa*), there is the seed-syllable *HŪṂ*. This pair, the seed-syllables of the God and Goddess, is transformed into Nairātmyā. From that [arises] Great Bliss; then the lotus, the support of bliss, the great passion, the giver of bliss, the portion, *HŪṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ*, the activity of Great Hatred, the Lord of Flavors, *HŪṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ*, the activity. Furthermore, externally, through the union of the churner and the churned, one should emit the circle of goddesses.

There, in the eastern and other doors, one should visualize Brahmā, Indra, Upendra, and Rudra in due order; likewise, in the corners beginning with the northeast, one should visualize the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), Nairṛti, and Vemacitrin.
Having thus visualized these eight seats, one should perceive the eight seed-syllables—*gaṃ*, *caṃ*, *vaṃ*, *ghaṃ*, *puṃ*, *saṃ*, *caṃ*, and *ḍaṃ*—within the union of moon and sun upon them.
From the transformation of these arise the emblems of Gaurī and the others: a curved knife (*kartī*), a skull-bowl (*kṛpīṭa*), a tortoise (*kūrma*), a serpent (*sarpa*), and a lion (*siṃha*).
One should visualize the circles of monks and vajras, and above them again those very same seed-syllables;
having transformed all these into one, Gaurī and the others are to be produced.
There, at the eastern gate, one should visualize Gaurī, born from the syllable *gaṃ*, black in color, holding a flaying knife in her right hand and a red lotus in her left,
treading upon Brahmā, and having the nature of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). And at the southern gate, Caurī, born from the syllable *caṃ*, of a madder-red color.
In her right hand she holds a fire-pan (*kṛpīṭa*) and in her left a boar;

mounted upon Indra, she is of the nature of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). At the western gate is Vettālī, born from the syllable *vaṃ*, with the luster of molten gold, holding a tortoise in her right arm and a lotus vessel in her left.

One should contemplate Ghasmarī at the northern gate, born from the syllable *ghaṃ*, having the nature of the aggregate of consciousness (*saṃjñā-skandha*), resembling an emerald, holding a snake in her right hand and a skull-cup in her left, mounted upon Rudra, and possessing the nature of the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). She is to be visualized as being stepped upon by Upendra.

In the northeast corner, one should visualize Pukkasī, born from the syllable Puṃ, blue in color, holding a lion in her right hand and an axe in her left, treading upon Vaivasvata, and having the nature of the earth element.

In the southeast, one should behold Śabarī, born from the syllable Śaṃ, white in color, holding a mendicant in her right hand and a jackal in her left, mounted upon a Khinkhirika, and having the nature of the water element.

In the southwest, one should visualize Caṇḍālī, born from the syllable Caṃ, with a sky-like dark complexion; she holds a wheel in her right hand and a plow in her left, and she is of the nature of the fire element, treading upon a Rākṣasa. In the northwest, one should visualize Ḍombinī, born from the syllable Ḍaṃ, of variegated color; she holds a vajra in her right hand and makes the threatening gesture (tarjanī) with her left, is mounted upon Vemacitrin, and is of the nature of the wind element.

All these [deities] should be meditated upon as having three eyes, mouths formidable with fangs, and upright tawny hair; they are naked, endowed with the five mudrās, standing in the dancing posture of half-lotus (ardhaparyaṅka), and produced from the emission of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta).

Immediately thereafter, the Blessed One, having become liquefied through union with his own consort by means of the singular flavor of the utterly intense and supreme great bliss, remained in the form of a seed-syllable.

Then the four goddesses, Pukkasī and the others, thinking "We are without a protector," fell into great despondency; being intensely longing, they roused the Blessed One with vajra-songs that awaken the mind.
Arise, O Bhairava! You who possess a compassionate mind, protect me! O Great Yogin, abandon desire for me; abandon this empty meditative absorption. If you leave me, I shall die. Arise, O Hevajra!

One should meditate on Dombinī in the northwest, born from the syllable DAṂ, having a variegated complexion, the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) as her nature, and possessing her own essential form. One should meditate on all [the goddesses] with faces upon faces.

The hair is adorned with mudrās; the hair remains in the supreme great [state]. Having fallen into great dejection, they are exceedingly distressed. They rouse her with songs: "Arise, O Maṇu! O Pukkasi! Protect me! O Mahāsuajoe! Cast off this honey! When you have abandoned it, the Void will be shaken; then you shall arise! Abandon the nature of the Void, O Sabarī! May the task be accomplished!"
"O Lord of Wine, though invited by me, why do you remain silent?
I am a Caṇḍālī; I entreat you, for without you, I cannot endure."
O Indī-ālī, arise! I know your heart;
we are Dombīs, so do not harbor such piteous thoughts.
Thus urged by these songs of reality (tattvagītikā), the Blessed One, like one awakened from sleep,
[beheld] that form of the moon consisting of flowing nectar,
above which were the two seed-syllables *huṃ* and *aṃ* arising from the two signs produced from the two seed-syllables.

Then, having condensed this entire solar disk into one, one should manifest oneself as the Blessed One, the illustrious Śrī Hevajra, arisen from the syllable *Hūṃ* and in union with Nairātmyā, who arises from the syllable *Aṃ*, in the center of the solar disk.
He is black in color, extremely fierce, with three eyes and tawny hair blazing upward;
his head is marked by a double-vajra (viśvavajra) above the forehead.

Adorned with a garland of five skulls, his face is formidable with a frown and knitted brows; the first face is black, the right is white, and the left is red. Furthermore, there are two black faces on the left and likewise two black faces on the right, while the upper face is smoke-colored and distorted.
All the faces indeed have fangs that are formidable and possess three eyes.

In the eight lotus-vessels situated in the eight right hands, there are, in order: an elephant, a horse, a donkey, a cow, a camel, a human, a dog, and a buffalo; likewise, in the eight skull-cups of the left hands, there are: Earth, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Tejas, Candra, Āditya, Yama, and Dhanada.

One should meditate on him as endowed with the six mudrās, his body adorned with a garland of fresh severed heads, naked, standing in the ālīḍha posture, treading upon the four Māras—Skanda, Kleśa, Mṛtyu, and Devaputra—standing in a dancing gesture upon a solar disc.
[Nairātmyā] is selfless, black, and two-armed;
she embraces the Blessed One with her right and left arms while holding a flaying knife and a skull-cup.
She is naked, adorned with the five mudrās, three-eyed, with tawny hair standing erect, her body decorated with a garland of severed human heads and a necklace of dried human skulls.
One should meditate upon the Blessed Lady as being in union with the Blessed Lord in the posture of *pratyālīḍha*, immersed in the flavor of the joy of supreme great bliss (*paramamahāsukha*).

Having thus clearly visualized, as previously described, the circle of the mandala situated within, surrounded by a host of vidyās, and filling the expanse of the sky with a mass of light rays, one should emit rays from the seed-syllable located in one's own heart;
having caused those rays to pervade the entire triple world, one should cause them to re-enter that very same syllable.

Again, having expanded the wheel of gnosis (jñānacakra) within the hollow of space, having drawn it forth, made it manifest before oneself, worshipped it, and praised it, one should bring it and cause it to enter one's own wheel of commitment (samayacakra).

Having caused [the deities] to enter and become one, and maintaining the divine pride (*devatāhaṃkāra*), one should visualize oneself being consecrated by Tathāgatas, Bodhisattvas, Vidyā-deities, Krodhas, and others, with vases filled with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) emerging from the mass of light rays issuing from one's own body, and being worshipped with various kinds of sublime offerings.

Thus, having pervaded the four moments—characterized respectively by the variegated (*vicitra*), the ripened (*vipāka*), the crushed (*vimarda*), and the signless (*vilakṣaṇa*)—and having focused upon the four joys (*ānanda*): joy (*ānanda*), supreme joy (*paramānanda*), cessation joy (*viramānanda*), and innate joy (*sahajānanda*), one should receive the four empowerments—the master, secret, wisdom, and the ultimate great bliss—through the fourfold purity of laughing, gazing, embracing, and union.
Having been empowered, one’s head is marked with the Lord of one’s own family.

Likewise, Gaurī and the others should be sealed by Cittavaśitā, Śāśvata, Ratnasaṃbhava, and Amitābha (319). Pukkasī and the others should be marked on the head by Dveṣa, Moha, Piśuna, and Rāga (320) (321).

And this Blessed One, together with his wheel, consists of the five gnoses; therein, the moon—which has the nature of the mirror-like wisdom—is produced from the transformation of the vowels (āli) (N₁ fol. 5vª; S 307r2; 307r6).
The sun, which has transformed into the letter *kā* and whose intrinsic nature is equanimity (*samatā*),
is the seed-syllable of the sign situated between those two; its thorough observation is *pratyavekṣaṇā*, and their transformation into one is *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna*.
The manifestation of the image is the thoroughly pure knowledge of the dharmadhātu.

Thus, [the sequence] of all the three realms—309, 317, *citteśa* (... *citteśa*, *śāśvata*, etc.—3180. [Note: *kramaṃ* is found in N₁, S, and EN; *kram* is in Ka.c., where a faint *ma* is still visible in the lower margin.]
And [the moments] characterized by the various ripenings and the distinct stages of dissolution;
pervading [all things].

Having understood that this [mandala] has the form of the mandala-circle (*maṇḍalacakra*) and has emerged from the bodhicitta produced by the great bliss of the single flavor of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*), one should contemplate that the eight goddesses, Gaurī and the others, have entered sequentially into one’s own eight faces.

Thus, having clearly perceived the single form of the entire triple world as consisting of wisdom and means, one should seal [the body] with the four wheels according to their respective locations. On the head is the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*), a lotus of thirty-two petals; in its pericarp, one should visualize a brilliantly shining white syllable *Haṃ*. At the throat is the enjoyment wheel (*saṃbhogacakra*), a lotus of sixteen petals; in its center is a red syllable *Oṃ*. At the heart is the dharma wheel (*dharmacakra*), an eight-petaled lotus; in its center is a blue syllable *Hūṃ*. At the navel is the emanation wheel (*nirmāṇacakra*), a sixty-four-petaled lotus; in its interior, one should meditate on the syllable *Aṃ* emitting five-colored rays. Having clearly visualized these wheels, one should expand the mass of their rays into the sky and cause them to dissolve back into those very wheels.

Then, by means of the Tathāgatas residing in the form of the six mudrās upon one's own body, one should armor oneself: Akṣobhya in the form of a wheel, Amitābha as earrings, Ratneśa on the neck-garland, and Vairocana situated in the hand. While resolving with the conviction that the entire triple world is the unity of wisdom and skillful means, one should don the armor. 328. 327. *samastatraidhātukaṃ* [N₁] / *samastaidhātuka* [S]; *samastatraidhātuka* [Ensil.. In the nose she is known as Mātsaryakī; in the mouth, Rāgavajrikā; in the body, Īrṣyāvajrī; and the mind is Nairātmyayoginī.

In the body, speech, and likewise in the mind, the seed-syllable is empowered upon the moon; one should recite the mantra *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*. Then one should meditate upon her who dwells in the sky, on the earth, and in the underworld (*pātāla*). Having performed worship, praise, and the tasting of nectar (*amṛtāsvāda*), and having thus become the pledge (*samaya*), the mantra is to be recited according to this procedure. Whatever mantra-syllables are uttered, having placed them in the body—*oṃ*.

One should dwell [upon] Vajrikā in the two ears, Vajrīkā in the mouth, Nairātmyā in the body, and Kāyabodhi in speech. One should recite the seed-syllable (*bīja*) empowered within the moon; one should meditate upon Khecarī, Bhūcarī, and Vāsinī. Then, having performed worship, praise, and the tasting of nectar (*amṛtāsvāda*), the *samaya* mantra is recited. By this procedure, whatever syllables are brought forth, they emerge from the mouths of the deities. Having caused them to enter one's own mouth with rays of light, they are emitted through the path of the *vajra*, enter the lotus of the Goddess, and again emerge from the mouths of the deities. In this sequence, one should rotate the mantra without interruption.

The distinction of caste should be established according to the distinction of karma. Having thus recited the mantra until exhaustion, one should then meditate upon a blue syllable *HŪṂ*—blazing and having the form of withdrawal—situated within the sun and moon at one’s own heart; one should perceive the syllable *AṂ* in the moon at the heart of Nairātmyā.
One should visualize the Blessed Lady, having become liquefied together with that very syllable *Aṃ* and the moon-maṇḍala, entering the heart of the Blessed Lord. Then the Blessed Lord also,

having emanated and reabsorbed [the deities] from the mass of rays issuing from the syllable *Hūṃ* situated within the moon and sun in his own heart— by means of the inhalation and exhalation of the *Ālikāli*— should perform the process of expansion and withdrawal.
Having entered that very place himself and become one with it, he remains in the state of the seed-syllable within the union of the moon and the sun.

Having emitted rays from the mouth of the deity, [the mantra] is cast forth through the path of the vajra and enters the lotus of the goddess. Again, from the mouth of the deity, in this sequence, the mantra should be recited without interruption; according to the distinction of the ritual action, a distinction of syllables should be made. Thus, without weariness, one should contemplate the *hūṃ* syllable within the mantra flashing forth from the heart. Having entered [the seed-syllable] *am*, *am*, *īm*, it emerges from within the sun with radiating rays. Expanding and contracting [these rays] through inhalation and exhalation, having caused them to enter and become unified, one remains in the state of the seed-syllable (*bījāvasthā*).

In this context, the following introduction should be remembered: "Neither beginning, nor end, nor middle; there is neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa. This is that supreme great bliss; neither other, nor self.

Having thus become of the nature of nectar through this seed-syllable, one should meditate—like a lamp flame—gradually transforming the moon and sun into the form of a mass of rays until they reach non-apprehensibility.
Thus, one should meditate according to the sequence of the four junctions (*catuḥsandhyā*), preceded by praise, worship, and the offering of *bali*.

Oṃ! Indra, Yama, Jala, Yakṣa, Yamajala, Yakṣa, Bhūta, Vahni, Vāyu, Rākṣasa, Candra, Sūrya, Māta, Bappa, Talapātāla, Aṣṭasarpa, svāhā! Neither existence nor nirvāṇa; neither the other nor this. By means of this seed-syllable: the two suns having become blended into the form of a mass of nectar, like a crest, [bestowing] attainment, in due order, preceded by the offering of the oblation—Oṃ! Indra, Yama, Yakṣa, Bhūta, Vāyu, Rākṣasa, Candra, Sūrya... Pātāla, Aṣṭa... Svāhā! Ātta! Enjoy this offering! Quickly! Flower, incense, meat, and perfume!
O Ambha, accomplish all tasks; O Khantikhunī, destroy the bonds! Om. The syllable *oṃ* is the mouth of all phenomena because they are primordially unarisen. *Oṃ āḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
The mantra for the bali offering to all beings:

Om! To the eight-faced one, whose tawny hair stands upright, who has twenty-four eyes and sixteen arms, whose body is like a black cloud, who wears many garlands of skulls, and whose mind is fierce and inflated with power.
To the one with fangs like a half-moon.
Slay! Cause to act! Roar! Threaten! Dry up the seven oceans!
Bind the eight nāgas! Seize the enemies—ha hā hi hī hu hū he hai ho hau ham haḥ phaṭ svāhā!
The root mantra of the Blessed One is: oṃ deva picuvajra hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
The heart mantra: Oṃ vajrakartari hevajrāya hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
The subsidiary heart mantra (upahṛdayamantra) is: oṃ a ka ca ṭa ta pa ya śa svāhā.
This is the mantra for agitating the city (purakṣobhamantra).

O Jihma, O Phulladhūpa, O Māṃsaviṅgha, O destroyer of all obstacles through patience! *Huṃ*! O Sarvapiṅgala, O four-faced one, O Jīmūtamālā! To the one of many garlands and cruel mind, *māraya* (slay), *garjaya* (roar) the enemies! *Hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ*! *Kartari*! At the time of the offering of the bali for worship from beginning to end, one should recite this supreme song of the pledge (*samayagītikā*), this supreme song of the pledge: "Kollaïre stands Bolā; Mummuṇire is Kakkolā. In the thick [forest] there is a cry of 'Ho!'; Karuṇe is made, not Rolā."
There, O friend, sweetmeats are eaten heartily;
there, O Kālindarī, wine is drunk; and there, the drum is beaten.
Four-leafed jasmine, *kacchurī*, *śilā*, and camphor are applied;
the fuel is *mālatī* flowers, and there *śāli* rice is eaten.
While making a manual calculation, one does not distinguish between pure and impure;
it is added to every limb without remainder, and there the result is subtracted.

At the time of the initial and final offerings and bali, one should recite this supreme song of the pledge (*samayagītikā*): "In Kollaire stands Bolā; in Mummunire is Kakkolā. In Ghane the drum resounds; in Karuṇe the offering is made. There, the bali is firmly established."

The drums are beaten here and there; the *causama* drums, the *cahusamā*, the *kacchuri*, the *sihlā*, the *sīhla*, the camphor, and the *gabbura* are sounded. The *mālai-indhana* incense, the *mālaï-indhana*, and the *śāliñja* rice are offered as fuel there and there. Food is eaten here and there; look! No one remains without food, for morsel after morsel is placed upon their bodies. There and there, the *sarāva* bowls, the *sarā*, the *sarāva*, and the *saravavi* vessels are washed. The *kunduru* incense is burned, and the *ḍiṇḍima* drums are sounded; yet, here they are not beaten.
The song should be sung in a low, warbling tone (kākalikā) in order to bring about the presence of all siddhis;
likewise, according to the sequence as prescribed, one should visualize the Blessed One situated within the mandala circle, with two arms and one face,
holding a vajra in his right hand and a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff in his left.
One should likewise visualize [the deity] in the ālīḍha posture, naked, trampling upon a corpse, with four arms,
holding a vajra in the right hand and a skull-cup in the left.
With his remaining two arms, he is embraced by his own consort; likewise, he has six arms and three faces—
the left face is red and the right face is white.

In his left hands he holds a trident and a bell; in his right hands, a vajra and a flaying knife. With his remaining two arms, he is embraced by his consort, who likewise embraces the Blessed One with her two arms holding a flaying knife and a skull-cup.
These [deities] have two, four, or six arms; they are blue in color,
possess three eyes,
have tawny hair standing erect, and are endowed with the six mudrās.
They should be visualized standing in the ālīḍha posture, naked, and treading upon corpses.
However, due to the absence of eight faces, one should cause the wheel of goddesses to enter into one's own body.

In the groves and in the forests, here and there, it does not blow; it is blown by the mantra-holder who bears the thunderbolt-bell. This mantra is recited by the mantra-holder: *Gata vajra vajra vāmamukha vāme dakṣiṇam dakṣiṇe śuklam śukla ghaṇṭam ghaṇṭā dakṣiṇe vajram vajra kartikām karttikā svābhavidyā vidyā karti katti kartri bhagavat bhagavantam*. They have two arms, four arms, or six arms; they have two arms, four arms, or six arms. Their colors are three-eyed; their colors are three-eyed. They are endowed with the six mudrās; they are endowed with the six mudrās. The feet, the body, the body—meditate on them, meditate on them as seated. *Oṃ trailokyākṣepa hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
The recitation mantra of the two-armed [deity].
Oṃ jvala jvalabhyaḥ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
This is the recitation mantra of the Four-Armed [Avalokiteśvara].
Oṃ kiṭi kiṭi vajra hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
This is the recitation mantra of the Six-Armed One.
The remainder should be performed as in the previous ritual procedure.
Furthermore, it should be understood in this way:
his eyes are red with compassion; he has a dark body due to a mind of loving-kindness; and his four feet are said to be the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
The eight faces are the eight liberations, and the sixteen arms are the sixteen emptinesses.
Through the [five] elements, there are the five Buddhas; he is wrathful for the sake of subduing the wicked.
Pukkasī is known by means of flesh, and Śabarī is conceived through blood.
The Caṇḍālī is in the form of semen; the Ḍombinī is in marrow and fat;

the skin is the seven factors of enlightenment; and the bone is the four truths—thus one should resolve. Having thus resolved, the practitioner should dwell in the yoga of the deity. And the aspiration is: *iHe Ta iHe Ta*. (cf. *VaPra* and others).

HeTa cf. VaPra et al.. HeTa cf. VaPra et al.. *Hum* *hum* *hum* *hum* *hum* *hum* *hum* *hum*. The remainder is like the ritual procedure (*vidhi*). And another thing should be understood in this way: with a red body from a mind of loving-kindness (*maitracitta*), the four [elements] are remembered; the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*) are the arms; by means of the measures (*mātrā*), they are the Buddhas from whom beings are to be trained. With flesh is Pukkasi, with semen is Dombinī; these four are thus born of the families (*kula*). One who is not insane, who observes the commitments (*samaya*), is a teacher of Hevajra.

May I be compassionate and devoted to my guru in birth after birth. (i) With vajra and bell ringing in my hands, may I be a profound reciter of the Dharma, taking up the semen of women in birth after birth. (ii)
Whatever has been written here by me, of dull intellect, through the force of faith, should be corrected by those who know the truth; and my faults should be forgiven with compassion by the virtuous.

The son of Śaśāṅkakulatilaka, a devotee of the lotus feet of his guru, composed this [work] by means of the circumstances he obtained; he who was not conquered by the enemy of pride, having performed the difficult-to-attain means of practice for the venerable Hevajra—
by whatever merit has been acquired by me through that, may the world become a bearer of the vajra.
The practical manual for the sādhana of Śrī Hevajra is completed. ||*|| ||
The work is by the venerable teacher Saroruhapāda. *HeTa* is also quoted in *HeSāSam*, *HeBāPūVi*, *SāMā*, and others.

"Life after life, birth after birth"—thus [it is said] in the *Hevajrabhaṭṭārakapāda-vivṛti*. "In birth after birth," "with speed," "with intellect"—[this refers to] that which is to be purified, whatever it may be, by those who know reality (*tattvajña*). And for me, by the virtuous ones (*sādhu*), out of compassion for beings (*sattvakṛpā*), O Moon! O Moon!—the tilaka has been made. That which was not conquered by me, by the enemy of pride (*abhimānaśatru*), in the lineage of the descent of pride (*abhimānāveśakula*)—that rare merit, auspicious merit, may Vajradhṛk [grant]. Thus ends the *Hevajra* [commentary]. Of the venerable feet... of him... thus. 131, 132.

Saroruhavajra’s *Hevajra*-lineage: having emanated Gaurī, Caurī, Vettālī—known as the Sun of the Self-Arisen Flower (svayambhūkusumākhyasurya)—Ghasmarī, Pukkasī, Śabarī, Caṇḍālī, and Dombī. [Citations from: *VaPra*, *HePra*, *DVS*, *HePra*, *HeTa* II.v, *HePra*, *VaPra*, *HePra*, *svayambhūkusumākhyasurya*, *śaivic*, *Picumata*, *Herukābhyudaya*, *HeSāUTib*.
She holds in her hand the flower called the "Self-Arisen Sun.
She is red according to the *Hevajra-sādhana* (CVSA) and the *Cakrasaṃvara-sādhana* (CVSB), and yellow according to the Tibetan version of the *Hevajra-sādhana* (HeSāU).

One should offer flowers, incense, lamps, divine food, and musical instruments in their respective order, [reciting] "The Lord" (*bhaṭṭāraka*) and "To the Lord Śrīhevajra" (*Śrīhevajrabhaṭṭārakasya*). [This is from] the *Cakravimśatikāstotra* of the *Hevajrasādhanopāyikā*, the ritual manual for the practice of *Hevajra*. (CVS VaPra HePra) — Annotated Translation, p. 133. (CVS Hong, Luo... Thus it is said: one should offer flowers, incense, lamps, divine food, and musical instruments in their proper sequence.
Furthermore, I offer myself to the mandala of glorious Hevajra together with its retinue; I pray that you accept me through your great compassion.
Then, one should also praise [the deity] with twenty verses of praise, and thereafter, one should confess one's misdeeds.

BRAHMAVIHĀRA-S: Having correctly analyzed [the nature of reality], one who is submerged in the ocean of conceptual construction should manifest great joy; being joyful, one is indifferent toward all imagined objects and so forth. Oṃ—recalling the aspiration, having visualized *su* and *ali*, having visualized *raṃ*, having visualized *nirū*, having visualized *nirū*, having visualized *nirū*, having visualized *pya*, having restrained the mind ending in *lyap*, having visualized *A*, and having established it firmly, [one realizes] the vajra-prajñā which is devoid of intrinsic nature.

Yaṃ. From consciousness (*vijñāna*), the maṇḍala circle suddenly appears clearly with the throat-signs: *Hūṃ*, *Āṃ*, Hevajra, *He*, *Kāra*, *DVS*. The circular form (*cakrākāra*)—the circular abode (*cakrāgāra*), the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*). *Oṃ oṃ padma*, giver of bliss (*sukhamdada*), great passion (*mahārāga*), *hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ oṃ vajra hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ*, the ritual of union (*suratavidhi*), the yoga of the churner and the churned (*manthamanthānayoga*).
Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Vaivasvata, Vittanāyaka, Nairṛti, Vemacitrin; gaṃ, caṃ, vaṃ, ghaṃ, puṃ, saṃ, caṃ, ḍaṃ;
Gaurī, Kārttikī, Cakrī, Vajrī.

One should visualize her standing upon Indra, red in hue with the color of a cochineal insect, holding a *camara* whisk in her left hand and likewise a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*) in her right, while embodying the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).
From the syllable *vaṃ*, one should visualize Vetālī, who has the luster of molten gold; she holds a tortoise in her right hand and a lotus vessel in her left.
One should contemplate her as being established in Viṣṇu, bearing the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha).
One should visualize Ghasmarī, who is green in color and has the luster of an emerald;
she holds a snake in her right hand and a skull-cup in her left,
and one should visualize her as abiding upon Rudra, embodying the aggregate of mental formations (saṃskāra-skandha).
From the syllable *puṃ* one should visualize Pukkasī, who is blue in color;
she holds a lion in her right hand and an axe in her left,
and she stands upon Vaivasvata while embodying the earth element.
One should visualize that Śabarī, who is white and of the same color [as the principal deity],
on the right [hand] holds a mendicant or a jackal in her hand,
while bearing a *khinkhirikā* (a small drum) and standing upon the Lord of Wealth (Kubera).
One should visualize Caṇḍālī, dark blue like a cloud and the color of a lotus,
holding a discus in her right hand and a plow in her left;
one should visualize her as possessing the fire element and stationed in the southwest.
One should visualize Ṭombinī, who has a variegated color, originating from the syllable Ḍaṃ; she holds a vajra in her right hand and likewise displays the tarjanī mudrā in her left,
while resting upon Vemācitrika and embodying the wind element.

Three-eyed, with faces pervading [the directions], with hair standing erect, tawny-hued, naked, wearing the five mudrās, engaged in the half-dance, born from the *bodhicitta*, arise, O Blessed One, O jewel of great compassion! Protect me, Pukkasi;
through the yoga of great bliss, grant me delight and abandon this samādhi of emptiness.
Without you I shall die! O Hevajra, arise! Abandon emptiness! Fulfill the task of Śabarī!
Having summoned all beings, why do you remain in emptiness, O Drinker of Wine? I, Caṇḍālī, entreat you; without you, no way out exists.
O Indīālī, arise! I know your mind; O Dombī, do not sever your compassionate heart!

HŪṂ AṂ: from the lunar disc, in the midst of the flowing liquid of nectar, are the two syllables HŪṂ and AṂ; from these arise two symbols. Then, having unified all of this together with their case endings, one should emanate oneself as the nature of Śrī Hevajra in the center of the circle of stars, the Blessed One arising from the syllable HŪṂ and Nairātmyā arising from the syllable AṂ.

One should visualize [the deity] as black in color, with a terrifying, loud laugh, three eyes, and tawny hair standing erect and pervading the upper sky; his head is marked by a vajra, he is adorned with a garland of five skulls, and his fangs are formidable and bared; his brows are knit in a frown. First, one should visualize the central face as black, the right as white, and the left as red; furthermore, two of the left faces are black and two of the right faces are black, while the face above is smoke-colored and distorted. All the faces have formidable fangs and three eyes.
In the eight southern lotus-vessels, there are, in sequence: the elephant, horse, donkey, snake, ox, man, dog, and jackal;
and in the eight northern lotus-vessels: earth, water, wind, fire, brilliance, moon, sun, Yama, and Kubera.
Adorned with six bones, his body decorated with a garland of nine skulls, naked, he stands in the *ālīḍha* posture.

One should visualize the four Māras—the Māra of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*), the Māra of the afflictions (*kleśa-māra*), the Māra of death (*mṛtyu-māra*), and the Māra who is the son of a god (*devaputra-māra*)—underfoot, as she dances in a wrathful manner upon a solar disc.

One should likewise visualize the Blessed Lady Nairātmyā, black in color, embracing [the central deity], holding a flaying knife (*kartṛkā*) and a skull-cup (*kapāla*) in her left and right hands. The five wisdoms: mirror-like, equality, discerning, all-accomplishing, and the wisdom of the sphere of phenomena (dharmadhātu). Having understood through resolute conviction, the single flavor of wisdom and skillful means; having perceived that which is to be contemplated, the wheel of great bliss; *haṃ*; *oṃ*; *hūṃ*; emanation—*aṃ*.

Saroruhavajra’s *Hevajra-lineage*: Akṣobhya is the wheel; Amitābha is the earring; Ratneśa is the necklace; Vairocana is the [third] eye; Amoghasiddhi is the vajra-holder. Mohavajrī is the nose; Dveṣavajrikā is the mouth; Mātsaryakī is the smell; Rāgavajrikā is the body; Īrṣyāvajrī is touch. Nairātmyayoginī—*Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ*. Khecarī, Bhūcarī, Pātālavāsinī. [End of] Pūjā and Stuti. *Hevajrasādhanopāyikā*—143, 37, 37.

The *yagītikā* *Padminī* (verse 43) says: *vajra* = thunderbolt; *ṭṭhia* = from the root √*sthā-*; *kollagiri nāḍi* = the channel (*nāḍi*) of the field (*kṣetra*) named Kollagiri; *kakkolā mummuṇi* = the channel of the field Kakkolā; *kiaï* = third person singular passive of the root √*kṛ-*; *ghaṇa* = continuously (*nirantaram*); *kibiḍa* = *kṛpīṭa* = a small drum (*ḍamaruka*); *rolā* = sound (*ārāva*) = a tumultuous noise (*kalakala*); *vājjaï* = third person singular passive of the root √*vrj-*.

*Padminī* 44: *māṃsa* (flesh); *khājjaï* = 3rd person singular passive of √*khad-*; *maaṇā* = *madhuna*, i.e., *bodhicitta*; *pijjaï* = √*pā-*; *gāḍhem* (deeply) = *nirbharam*; *kāliñjara* = *bhavya*, *samayin*; b) = *pra√nī-*; *dunduru* = *asamayin*, [one who has not taken] vows. *HeTa I.ii. 3. xi; HeTa I.ii. 22.*

Spicy sauce: *causama*, *catuḥsama*, urine (*kacchuri* = *kasturikā*, musk), blood (*sihlā* = *sihlaka*, olibanum), semen (*kāppura* = *karpūra*, camphor)—the *yo-mā-skandhas*; *lāiaï* = 3rd person plural passive of the root *Vlabh-*; *mālaïïndhaṇa* (jasmine wood) as the condiment (*vyañjana*); *śālia*, *śāliñja* (rice) as the *mahāmāmsa*; *khāiaï* = 3rd person plural passive of the root *Nkhad-*; *bharu* = abundant (*pracuram*).

46. While performing the visualization (*prekṣaṇa*) and the field (*kṣetra*), [one contemplates] the coming and going (*āgatigati*; cf. *YoMā*). "Pure" (*śuddha*) refers to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*); "impure" (*aśuddha*) refers to the beginner (*ādikarmika*). *Muṇiaï* is the third person singular passive of the root *√man*. *Aṅge caḍābiaï* means "it is placed upon the limbs" (*aṅgeṣu āropyate*). *Niramsu* means "without clothes" (*nir-amsuka*, i.e., naked) and refers to the bone ornaments (*asthyābharaṇa*). *Sarāba* is *śrāyas*, meaning "resort"; *sava* refers to the selflessness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmanairātmya*).

*Malaya-ja* = *malayaja* (sandalwood); *milana* = *melaka* (meeting); *kunduru*; *vāṭai* = *vartate* (it exists/occurs); *ḍiṇḍima-samādhi*; *ṇa vājjiaï* = √*vrj-* (YoMā: it is not made one's own). xiii HeTa II.iv. 6–8; see Appendix. *om trailokyākṣepa-hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. xiv *om jvalajvalābhyaḥ-hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*, *om kiti kiti vajra hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. [This is performed] by means of the four bases of sympathy (*saṃgrahavastu*), namely: generosity (*dāna*), pleasant speech (*priyavacana*), purposeful action (*arthacaryā*), and consistency of purpose (*samānārthatā*).
Aspiration: Having become intent [on this], he who partakes of the semen of a woman is the Holder of the Vajra, the Knower of Reality, the Means for the Sadhana of Hevajra.
